growth_story.headline: Myanmar's income per person grew fast for two decades, then the pandemic, the 2021 coup, conflict and an earthquake erased a decade of gains.
growth_story.arc: Myanmar's income per person grew 4.2 percent a year over 1990–1998, while the country stayed largely closed to the world and under Western sanctions. Growth then ran at 11.3 percent a year over 1999–2009, as gas exports came fully on stream, though the World Bank has said the official growth figures from those years do not fit the rest of the economy. After political and economic reforms opened the country in 2011, growth held at 6.4 percent a year over 2010–2017, and was still 5.5 percent in 2018 and 5.8 in 2019. The pandemic and the February 2021 military takeover then cut income per person by 9.7 percent in 2020 and 12.6 percent in 2021, and after a small rebound in 2022, conflict, the March 2025 earthquake and power shortages pushed it down again in 2024 and 2025, so the 2018–2025 era averaged -1.5 percent a year. By 2025 income per person was 21.7 percent below its 2019 peak, about where it first was in 2015.

threads.title: Isolation, sanctions and gas
threads.text: For decades Myanmar was closed to most of the world and under Western sanctions, with trade and investment limited to a few neighbours. Gas exports, in full flow from 2002, brought in foreign currency during the fast 1999–2009 era. The World Bank later judged the official growth figures from those years hard to square with the rest of the economy.

threads.title: Opening up after 2011
threads.text: Political and economic reforms from 2011 opened the economy and growth stayed strong through the 2010s. That growth leaned on a narrow base of natural resource exports, building and tourism.

threads.title: Pandemic and military takeover
threads.text: The pandemic hit first in 2020, then the February 2021 military takeover brought protests, labour shortages and disruption to business services such as logistics and telecoms. Income per person fell 9.7 percent in 2020 and 12.6 percent in 2021.

threads.title: Conflict and lost jobs
threads.text: By late 2024 more than half of the country's townships saw active fighting, which disrupted supply chains and border trade. The World Bank finds conflict is likely reversing the usual path of development, with even skilled workers moving into low-paid farm work.

threads.title: Earthquake and power cuts
threads.text: The March 2025 earthquake closed factories, broke supply chains and damaged infrastructure, on top of conflict and power shortages, and output fell again. Thin money for rebuilding, insecurity and unreliable electricity still hold back the recovery.

since_last_year.text: After the March 2025 earthquake the economy steadied a little: firms worked closer to capacity by late 2025, and some power shortages eased into early 2026. Then a fuel shock from Middle East tensions in early 2026 added to the strain. The data show income per person fell 2.6 percent in 2025.

citations.title: Myanmar's Economy shows tentative stabilization, but fuel shock intensifies pressures

citations.title: Myanmar's Economy shows tentative stabilization, but fuel shock intensifies pressures
citations.quote: A fuel shock driven by Middle East tensions in early 2026 has amplified existing economic pressures.

growth_story.tension: The data put growth in income per person at 11.3 percent a year over 1999–2009, the fastest of the four eras since 1990, but the World Bank has said Myanmar's historical official growth rates do not fit the economy's fundamentals or the data from key sectors. The boom of that era may be smaller than the data show.
